14360:
"Seedy" describes something — a place, a person, an atmosphere, or a situation — that feels dirty, run-down, and morally questionable all at once. It is not just about being physically messy or old. It carries a strong sense of disreputability — the feeling that something shady, shambolic, or even slightly criminal is going on there.

Think of it this way: a neglected old building is not automatically "seedy." But a neglected old building where suspicious things happen, where you wouldn't want to be alone at night, where the walls are stained and the lighting is dim and the people there look shifty — that is seedy.
Meaning 1: Shabby, Dirty, and Run-Down (Physical Appearance)

When "seedy" describes a place, it paints a picture of visible neglect and decay. The place looks like it hasn't been cared for in a long time. It is grimy, poorly lit, cheaply furnished, and worn out.

But what separates "seedy" from simply "dirty" or "old" is the feeling it creates. A seedy place does not just look bad — it makes you feel uncomfortable and unsafe. There is an air of unpleasantness hanging over it.

Examples:

  • "They met in a seedy motel on the edge of the city — the kind with broken neon signs and curtains that didn't quite close."
  • "She walked through a seedy alley full of overflowing bins and graffiti-covered walls."
  • "The office was above a seedy bar that smelled of stale beer and cigarettes."

Typical seedy places include: run-down motels, dimly lit bars, neglected back-alley streets, cheap clubs in rough parts of a city.
Meaning 2: Morally Questionable and Disreputable (Character and Atmosphere)

This is where "seedy" becomes richer and more interesting. It is not just about looking bad — it is about being morally dubious.

A "seedy" person, deal, activity, or business is one that feels dishonest, shady, corrupt, or of low moral character. It suggests something you would not want to openly associate with. It is the kind of thing people do in secret, behind closed doors, in the dark. It hints at illegal activity, exploitation, or deeply questionable behavior.

Examples:

  • "He had a seedy reputation in the industry — everyone knew he cut corners and paid people under the table."
  • "The politician's seedy past — involving bribery and forged documents — finally came to light."
  • "There was something seedy about the whole arrangement that she couldn't quite put her finger on."
  • "The website had a seedy feel to it — like it was designed to deceive you."

Notice how "seedy" here is not just about appearance but about character and ethics. A person can be well-dressed and clean but still described as seedy if their behavior is corrupt, exploitative, or morally reprehensible.
How These Two Meanings Work Together

In practice, the physical and moral senses of "seedy" are deeply intertwined. A "seedy part of town" is both physically run-down and associated with crime, prostitution, drug-dealing, or other morally undesirable activities. The physical seediness reflects and reinforces the moral seediness.

This is what makes "seedy" such a vivid word. It captures an atmosphere — a whole mood — in one word. It says: this place (or person) is grimy, neglected, untrustworthy, and operating in the shadows.

Examples that show both meanings together:

  • "The detective followed the suspect into a seedy part of town, past boarded-up shops and men loitering in doorways."
  • "They arranged the deal in a seedy casino — the kind frequented by people who preferred to stay off the radar."

In British English, "seedy" has an additional, completely separate meaning: feeling slightly ill, unwell, or off-colour. This meaning has nothing to do with places or moral character.

If someone says "I'm feeling a bit seedy today," they mean they feel under the weather — perhaps a bit nauseous, tired, or generally not their best. It is a mild, informal way of saying you are not feeling well.

Examples:

  • "He looked seedy — pale and tired, with dark circles under his eyes."
  • "I ate something strange last night and I've been feeling seedy all morning."

This meaning is less commonly used in American English, so if you are speaking to a British person and they say they feel "seedy," do not assume they are calling themselves disreputable!

"Seedy" sits in a particular range of severity. It is worse than merely shabby or rough, but not as extreme as words like "depraved" or "criminal." It is the grey zone — not outright evil, but definitely not wholesome. It implies the kind of activities that are either technically illegal, morally questionable, or at least embarrassing.

It often carries a slightly judgmental tone — the speaker is passing quiet moral judgment on the person or place.

It is worth being clear about what seedy does not mean:

  • It does not mean simply poor or low-income. A poor neighborhood is not necessarily seedy. Seediness requires that additional layer of moral degradation or disrepute.
  • It does not mean just old or worn. An antique shop full of dusty old things is not seedy. A pawnshop in a rough neighborhood where stolen goods are quietly traded — that is seedy.
  • It is not the same as "dangerous." A war zone is dangerous, not seedy. Seedy is more about moral seediness — small-scale corruption, vice, and disreputability.
  • It does not necessarily mean violent. Seedy places can be quiet and low-key. The danger in a seedy environment is often more social and moral than physical.

"Seedy" is an informal adjective with a slightly journalistic, atmospheric quality. It is frequently used in fiction, journalism, and everyday speech to quickly paint a vivid picture of a morally compromised environment or character. It almost always carries a negative judgment from the speaker.

It is the kind of word used to describe the world of private investigators, back-alley deals, cheap motels, corrupt local officials, or old noir movies. If you have ever read a detective novel or watched a crime drama — anywhere with shadowy characters and dirty back streets — you are in the territory of "seedy."

Physical senseDirty, run-down, neglected, cheap-looking, with an air of discomfort and unease
Moral senseDisreputable, shady, corrupt, ethically questionable, associated with vice or small-time crime
British informal senseFeeling slightly unwell or under the weather
Overall feelJudgmental, atmospheric, slightly literary; used to describe places, people, deals, or situations operating in the moral grey zone

If you remember just one thing: seedy = shabby on the outside + shady on the inside. It is a word that wrinkles its nose slightly at something it finds both physically unappealing and morally questionable.
14361:
"Seemingly" means "in a way that appears to be true or real, but may or may not actually be so."

It is the adverb form of the adjective "seeming," which itself comes from the verb "to seem" (= to appear, to give an impression of).

When you use "seemingly," you are describing how something looks on the surface — while quietly keeping open the possibility that the reality underneath could be different.

Think of "seemingly" as a soft warning: "This is what it looks like — but I'm not fully sure it's true."

It sits between two things:

  • What something appears to be
  • What it might actually be

The word lives in that gap.

"The task was seemingly impossible, but she finished it in an hour."

Here, the task looked impossible at first glance. That was the surface impression. But it turned out not to be. The word "seemingly" told you in advance: don't fully trust this appearance.

"He was seemingly calm, but his hands were shaking."

His outward appearance said: calm. But the reality — the shaking hands — said something else. "Seemingly" flags the gap between the two.

"The two events are seemingly unrelated."

This doesn't say they ARE unrelated. It says: based on first look, they appear unrelated. Maybe they are. Maybe they aren't. The speaker isn't committing either way.
Why This Word Exists (and Why It Matters)

Without "seemingly," language would force you to either:

  • State something as a fact: "The task was impossible."
  • State outright doubt: "I don't know if the task was impossible."

"Seemingly" gives you a middle path. You can describe an appearance accurately and honestly, without pretending to know the full truth. This is why careful writers — journalists, scientists, academics — use it often. It is a word of intellectual honesty.

"Seemingly" carries mild-to-moderate doubt. It doesn't scream "this is definitely false!" It simply raises a quiet eyebrow.

Compare:

  • "He is happy." → You're stating a fact.
  • "He is seemingly happy." → You're noting the appearance, with a hint that reality might differ.
  • "He is pretending to be happy." → You're asserting the appearance is false.

"Seemingly" sits in the middle of that range, closer to neutral observation than outright contradiction.
Where It Goes in a Sentence

"Seemingly" is almost always placed right before the word or phrase it modifies:

  • Before an adjective: "a seemingly perfect plan" / "seemingly unimportant details"
  • Before an adverb phrase: "seemingly without effort" / "seemingly at random"
  • Before a verb: "The road seemingly had no end."

It is rarely placed at the end of a sentence. It needs to sit close to what it is qualifying.

A very frequent pattern is:

"seemingly [negative/difficult thing]" → followed by a surprising reality

  • "a seemingly unsolvable problem" (but it was solved)
  • "a seemingly ordinary day" (but something extraordinary happened)
  • "seemingly unrelated events" (but they turned out to be connected)

This pattern is so common because "seemingly" is often used to set up contrast — to describe an appearance before revealing a different truth.

But it also works without any contrast, simply as honest caution:

  • "The company is seemingly profitable." (This is what the numbers suggest, though I can't be fully certain.)

Apparently — very close in meaning, and often interchangeable. However, "apparently" can also mean "based on what someone told me" (hearsay), not just "based on how it looks." "Seemingly" sticks more purely to observable appearance.

"He apparently left early." → Someone told me this, or I noticed signs of it.
"He seemingly left early." → Based on observable evidence (empty chair, coat gone), it appears so.

Ostensibly — more formal and carries a stronger suggestion that the outward appearance is deliberately masking something else. It has a mild hint of deception or pretense.

"He was ostensibly there to help, but he was actually spying."

"Seemingly" is more neutral — it doesn't imply any deception. It simply notes an appearance.

"Seemingly" is a moderately formal word. You will see it often in:

  • Journalism and news writing
  • Academic writing and research
  • Formal essays and analysis
  • Literary fiction

In casual conversation, people more often say "it seems like," "apparently," or "looks like." Saying "seemingly" in everyday speech is not wrong — it just sounds slightly formal.

"Seemingly" means: "based on outward appearance or first impressions, this appears to be the case — but reality may differ."

It is a word of careful observation. It describes the surface without claiming to know the depth. When you see it in a sentence, it is a signal: look carefully — things may not be exactly as they appear.
14362: "Seemly" describes behavior, actions, speech, or appearance that is proper, fitting, and appropriate — especially in a social or public setting. When something is seemly, it matches what is considered decent, dignified, and in good taste for the situation at hand.
The central idea: fitting the moment

Every situation in life — a funeral, a formal ceremony, a job interview, a place of worship — carries unwritten expectations about how a person should behave, speak, and carry themselves. When someone meets those expectations gracefully and with dignity, their conduct can be called seemly. It signals that the person understands the context they are in and is acting in a way that feels right, respectful, and harmonious.

It's not just about following rules mechanically. "Seemly" carries a sense of grace — the feeling that everything is as it should be, that nothing is jarring or out of place.

• Speaking in a hushed, respectful tone at a memorial service is seemly.
  • Dressing modestly for a religious ceremony is seemly.
  • Responding to a public insult with calm and measured words is a seemly response.
  • For a judge to maintain a composed and impartial manner in court is entirely seemly.

Notice that in each case, the behavior fits — it aligns with the dignity, norms, and spirit of the occasion.

"Seemly" is not just about social etiquette (following rules to avoid awkwardness). It carries a slight moral weight too. It points to behavior that is genuinely proper and respectful — the kind that reflects good character and consideration for others, not merely what is fashionable or convenient.

This is what makes "seemly" richer than the word "appropriate." Something can be appropriate in a narrow, technical sense — a correctly worded email, for example — without being seemly. Seemly implies a fuller kind of rightness: the right action, done in the right spirit, in the right manner.

The word can apply to many things:

  • Behavior and conduct — how a person acts
  • Speech and language — the words and tone someone chooses
  • Dress and appearance — how someone presents themselves
  • A response or reaction — how someone handles a situation
  • The general manner or bearing of a person — the overall impression they give
Register: a formal, somewhat old-fashioned word

"Seemly" is not everyday casual language. You won't typically hear it in informal conversation. It appears mostly in formal writing, literature, religious or ceremonial contexts, and careful speech. It is perfectly correct and understood today, but it has a dignified, traditional tone to it. Think of it as the kind of word you might find in a classic novel or a formal sermon.

Interestingly, the negative form — "unseemly" — is used far more frequently in modern English than "seemly" itself. If something is unseemly, it is improper, undignified, or out of place in a way that makes onlookers uncomfortable or disapproving.

  • Laughing loudly at a solemn occasion is unseemly.
  • An unseemly quarrel broke out between the two politicians.
  • It was considered unseemly for a person of her position to behave so recklessly.

Keeping "unseemly" in mind is helpful: if unseemly behavior makes people feel that something is wrong, seemly behavior makes people feel that everything is as it should be.

To be precise, it's worth noting what the word does not mean:

  • It does not mean "beautiful" or "physically attractive," although a seemly appearance implies dignity.
  • It does not simply mean "legal" or "permitted" — something can be entirely legal and still be deeply unseemly.
  • It is not purely about formality. Even relaxed, informal situations have their own standards for what is seemly. Cracking a crude joke with close friends at an informal gathering might be perfectly seemly; doing the same at a dignified public event would not be.
  • It is not about personal preference alone — it refers to shared social and moral standards, not just one person's taste.

What is seemly in one culture, community, or situation may not be seemly in another. The word always implies a standard, but that standard is defined by the setting and the people involved. What matters is whether the behavior aligns with the values and expectations of the specific context at hand.

This is why "seemly" is never an absolute judgment — it always asks: proper and fitting for this occasion, this place, and these people?

Seemly = proper, fitting, and appropriate in terms of social and moral conduct — the kind of behavior that belongs to the occasion, reflects dignity and good taste, and makes those around you feel that all is as it should be.
14363:
To seep means to move slowly, quietly, and gradually through very small openings, cracks, pores, or gaps — almost as if the substance is squeezing itself through a surface that wasn't really designed to let it pass.

Think of it this way: when something seeps, it doesn't rush, pour, or gush. It barely moves. It is a soft, almost invisible kind of movement — slow enough that you might not even notice it happening until it has already happened.
The Two Key Qualities of Seeping

If you remember only two things about this word, remember these:

  1. Slowness — Seeping is never fast. The moment movement becomes quick or forceful, we stop calling it seeping.
  2. Through tiny spaces — Something seeps through a material, into a surface, or out of a substance — always through very small gaps, pores, or cracks, not through a wide-open hole.

This is where the word is most commonly used — to describe liquids (or sometimes gases) moving through solid materials.

  • Water seeps through soil after rain. The water doesn't stay on top — it slowly works its way down through the tiny spaces between soil particles.
  • If you have a small crack in a wall, moisture from outside seeps into the wall. You don't see it flooding in; you only notice the wall is damp days later.
  • Blood can seep through a bandage if the wound is not fully healed. The cloth absorbs it, slowly.
  • Oil sometimes seeps out of the ground naturally at certain locations. It doesn't erupt like a geyser — it oozes up slowly from underground.
  • Gas can seep through the cracks of a poorly sealed pipe.
  • Cold air seeps through the gaps around an old window frame in winter.

Notice how in every case, the movement is slow, gradual, and passes through something that is not wide open.

"Seep" is also widely used to talk about non-physical things — emotions, feelings, thoughts, information — when they enter or spread slowly and quietly. This is a very natural extension of the word's core idea.

  • Fear seeped into her mind as the night grew darker. — Fear didn't arrive all at once like a shock; it crept in gradually and quietly.
  • Doubt began to seep into his confidence. — His confidence wasn't shattered suddenly; small doubts quietly started getting in.
  • The truth slowly seeped out. — The truth wasn't revealed all at once; it came out little by little over time.
  • Sadness had seeped into every corner of the house after the loss. — A slow, quiet spread of sadness throughout a place.
  • News of the scandal seeped out before the official announcement. — Information leaked out slowly, through informal channels.

The figurative use always keeps the same essence: something entering, spreading, or escaping slowly, quietly, and gradually.

Interestingly, "seep" is also used with light, even though light isn't a liquid:

  • Pale morning light seeped through the curtains. — A small, soft amount of light was coming through the curtains, quietly and gradually, as if filtering through.
  • A thin line of yellow light seeped under the closed door.

This works because the visual image matches the word perfectly — a little bit of something, moving slowly through a narrow gap.
Common Directions: Into, Out, Through, Away

The word "seep" is almost always followed by a preposition, and the preposition changes what exactly is happening:

  • Seep into — something is entering slowly: Water seeped into the basement.
  • Seep out — something is escaping slowly: Gas seeped out of the old pipes.
  • Seep through — something is passing completely through a material: The dye seeped through the fabric.
  • Seep away — something is gradually disappearing or draining: His hope seeped away with every passing day. / The water seeped away into the ground.
  • Seep down / up — direction of movement: Rainwater seeped down through the layers of rock.
How Seep Differs from Similar Words

Understanding what makes "seep" different from similar words will sharpen your understanding considerably.

Seep vs. Leak:
"Leak" suggests an unintended escape of a substance through a specific point of failure (a hole, a crack). It can be faster than seeping and is typically used for a more noticeable flow. A pipe leaks when there's a hole; moisture seeps through a wall over time. Both involve unwanted passage, but leaking is more sudden and noticeable; seeping is more gradual and quiet.

Seep vs. Flow:
"Flow" implies an open, smooth, unobstructed movement — like a river flowing. There is no barrier being penetrated. Seeping, by contrast, always involves squeezing through something.

Seep vs. Drip:
"Drip" describes drops falling downward. It is about drops and falling. Seeping is about passing through a surface, not necessarily downward, and not in drops.

Seep vs. Ooze:
These are the closest pair. "Ooze" also means to move slowly, but it carries a thicker, stickier, more viscous quality — like mud, blood, or slime oozing. It often feels more unpleasant. "Seep" is cleaner and more neutral. Water seeps; pus or slime oozes.

Seep vs. Trickle:
"Trickle" is a thin, narrow stream flowing (usually downward). It is slightly faster and more visible than seeping. A trickle is on a surface; seeping is through a surface.

"Seep" has a quiet, unhurried, almost unstoppable quality to it. Things that seep don't ask for permission — they just slowly, persistently make their way through. This is why it works so well in figurative language too. When we say "doubt seeped in," we mean it wasn't dramatic; it was patient, quiet, and by the time you noticed it, it was already there.

• After the heavy rain, water seeped into the foundation of the house.
  • The smell of fresh bread seeped out from the bakery and into the street.
  • She could feel exhaustion seeping through her body after the long hike.
  • The ink seeped through the thin paper, leaving a stain on the page beneath.
  • Over the years, cynicism had slowly seeped into his once-optimistic heart.
  • Warm light seeped through the gap in the curtains, landing on the floor in a thin stripe.
  • The oil spill allowed crude oil to seep into the ocean floor.
  • As weeks passed, the excitement of the new job began to seep away.
  • Classified information had been seeping out to journalists for months.
  • Cold was seeping in through the broken window seal.

To seep = to pass slowly and gradually through small openings, pores, or gaps. It is used for liquids, gases, light, and even abstract things like emotions or information. The defining qualities are slowness, gradualness, and passage through tight or tiny spaces. It is never fast, never forceful, and often describes a process you barely notice while it's happening.
14364:
A seer is a person who sees things that ordinary people cannot see — specifically, things that are hidden, distant in time, or beyond the reach of normal human senses. The word is built on the simple act of seeing, but pushed far beyond the physical: a seer doesn't just see with their eyes, they see with something deeper — a kind of inner or supernatural vision.

The most essential thing to understand about a seer is this: they perceive what is invisible to others. That "invisible" thing is usually the future, but it can also be hidden truths about the present or past.
The Primary Meaning: A Person with Prophetic Vision

In its most common and important sense, a seer is someone who is believed to have the supernatural gift of seeing visions — especially visions of future events. They don't reason or calculate their way to a prediction the way a scientist or analyst might. Instead, they receive knowledge, often through dreams, trances, or vivid mental visions that come to them unbidden.

A seer doesn't go looking for the future with logic. The future, in a sense, comes to them.

Example: In ancient times, kings would consult seers before going to war. The seer would enter a trance-like state and report what they saw — a great victory, a crushing defeat, a betrayal.

This meaning is ancient and appears across virtually every human culture throughout history. From the oracles of ancient Greece to the prophets of the Bible to the shamans of indigenous traditions — the seer is a universal human idea.
How a Seer Differs from Similar Words

These words are closely related but not identical:

Prophet: A prophet is someone who delivers a divine message or warning, often on behalf of a god or higher power. The emphasis is on speaking or declaring. A seer's emphasis is on seeing — the vision comes first. In practice, many prophets in religious texts are also called seers, and the words overlap heavily. But if you had to separate them: a seer receives a vision; a prophet delivers a message. A seer sees; a prophet speaks.

Oracle: An oracle is typically a place or institution through which divine knowledge is communicated (like the Oracle at Delphi in ancient Greece), or the utterance itself — the cryptic answer given. A seer is always a person.

Fortune-teller: A fortune-teller is a broader, more casual term for anyone who claims to predict your personal future, often using tools like tarot cards, a crystal ball, or reading palms. A fortune-teller has a more commercial, street-fair connotation. The word "seer" carries far more gravity, awe, and reverence. You'd call a great biblical figure a seer; you wouldn't call them a fortune-teller.

Visionary: A visionary is someone with remarkable imagination and foresight — they can envision a future others can't. But a visionary achieves this through intelligence and creative thinking, not supernatural perception. A seer's insight is treated as given to them from beyond; a visionary's insight is treated as produced by their own exceptional mind.

In modern, everyday English, "seer" is also used figuratively — as a compliment or metaphor — for anyone who seems to predict the future with uncanny accuracy, even without any supernatural claim.

Example: "The economist who predicted the financial crash of 2008 years before it happened was hailed as a seer."

Here, the writer isn't claiming the economist had mystical powers. They're saying: this person saw clearly what everyone else was blind to, and that deserves the highest praise we can give to foresight. The word "seer" is chosen deliberately for its weight and reverence.

This figurative use is common in journalism and literary writing. When someone calls a tech entrepreneur a "seer," or a philosopher a "seer of human nature," they mean: this person saw true things before others could.

Very occasionally, in formal or archaic writing, "seer" is used in its most stripped-down literal sense: simply one who sees. As in, a person who is physically capable of seeing (as opposed to someone who is blind). This usage is extremely rare in modern English and mostly appears in old texts or poetic contexts. You will almost never encounter "seer" used this way in contemporary writing.

The word "seer" carries a powerful emotional weight. It suggests:

  • Rarity: Not everyone is a seer. It implies a special, extraordinary gift.
  • Gravity: It is a serious word. It's not playful or trivial.
  • Reverence: Seers have historically been treated with awe, sometimes fear, often deep respect.
  • Mysticism: It lives in the world of the spiritual and the supernatural, not the scientific.
  • Loneliness or burden: In stories and mythology, seers often suffer because they see terrible things coming and cannot stop them. The Greek figure Cassandra, for instance, was cursed to see the future truly but never to be believed — a tragic version of the seer.

When you call someone a seer, you are placing them in the same category as oracles, prophets, and visionaries who have shaped how civilizations understood the world.

SituationIs "seer" appropriate?

If someone has a gift — real or believed — for seeing the future through visions and inner sight, they are a seer in the full, traditional sense. If someone is merely very good at predicting things through intelligence and observation, they might be called a seer figuratively, as a high compliment. If someone tells your fortune at a carnival, you'd more likely call them a fortune-teller than a seer, because "seer" implies something grander and more respected. And if the word appears in an old text simply meaning "someone who sees with their eyes," that is an archaic usage worth recognizing but not worrying about much.

The heart of the word is always the same: a seer sees what others cannot. Whether that vision is supernatural, spiritual, or simply extraordinary insight into how the world works — to call someone a seer is to say they possess a kind of perception that most human beings lack.
14365: Seersucker is a type of cloth — specifically, a lightweight fabric known for its distinctive bumpy, crinkled surface texture.
What makes it unique: the texture

If you've ever looked at a fabric that has alternating stripes of bumpy, puckered (crinkled) sections and smooth, flat sections, that's seersucker. Run your hand across it and you'll feel the surface rise and fall in a gentle, wavy pattern.

This crinkled texture isn't a defect, an accident, or the result of bad washing. It's woven deliberately into the fabric during manufacturing. The way it's made: during weaving, some threads are held slack (loose) while others are held tight. The slack threads bunch up and pucker, creating those raised ridges, while the tighter threads stay flat. The two sets alternate, giving seersucker its signature striped, rippled appearance.

This texture is permanent — it doesn't wash out or iron out. In fact, you're not supposed to iron seersucker at all, because ironing would flatten the puckers and ruin what makes the fabric special.

The most iconic, classic version of seersucker is blue and white stripes — you've likely seen it on a summer suit or shirt. But seersucker comes in many color combinations: pink and white, green and white, red and white, multicolor plaids, checks, and so on. The stripes run lengthwise along the fabric.

Seersucker is most commonly made from cotton, which makes it breathable and comfortable. It can also be made from polyester, silk, or a blend of fibers — but cotton seersucker is the most traditional and widely used.
Why it exists: the practical purpose

Seersucker was designed for hot, humid weather, and it solves a specific problem: in heat, most fabrics cling to your skin, trapping warmth and making you uncomfortable.

Seersucker's puckered texture means the fabric doesn't lie flat against your skin. The raised ridges and bumps create tiny air pockets between the cloth and your body. Air circulates through these gaps, pulling heat and moisture away. The result: you feel noticeably cooler wearing seersucker than you would wearing a similarly thin but flat fabric.

As a bonus, because the fabric is already textured and crinkled, wrinkles are essentially invisible on seersucker. A flat fabric shows every crease and wrinkle clearly — but on seersucker, the existing texture masks them. This makes it a very low-maintenance, travel-friendly fabric.

Clothing is the primary use:

  • Suits (jackets and trousers worn together as a matching set)
  • Blazers and sport coats
  • Trousers and shorts
  • Shirts and blouses
  • Dresses and skirts
  • Children's clothing

It's also used for home textiles like bedsheets, pillowcases, duvet covers, curtains, and sometimes bags or accessories.
When and where you'd encounter it

Seersucker is a warm-weather fabric — you'll see it in spring and summer collections. Wearing seersucker in cold weather would look out of place, since it's so strongly associated with warmth and heat.

It has a particularly strong association with the American South, where hot, humid summers made it practically essential. Seersucker suits became a symbol of Southern gentlemen's summer fashion — elegant yet sensible. This association spread and seersucker suits became a broader American warm-weather classic.

In the United States Senate, there is a long-standing tradition called "Seersucker Thursday" (held once a year in June), where senators wear seersucker suits to the Senate floor as a nod to this heritage.
The feel of seersucker in one sentence

If you've never touched it: imagine a lightweight cotton fabric that feels slightly textured and bumpy under your fingers — not scratchy, but gently ridged — that hangs loosely and doesn't cling, keeping you cool and looking clean even on the hottest days. That's seersucker.
14366:
To seethe means to be in a state of intense, turbulent, barely-contained agitation — like something that is violently churning and boiling on the inside.

That image of boiling is the perfect mental anchor for this word. Think of a pot of water at a rolling boil — churning, bubbling furiously, full of violent energy, threatening to spill over. That is exactly what seethe captures, whether it's describing a liquid or a feeling inside a person.

1. Literal — A liquid boiling or bubbling violently

In its literal sense, seethe describes liquid that is churning and bubbling with great force. This is the oldest use of the word, and while it's rare in everyday modern speech, you'll still encounter it in literature and formal writing.

  • The lava seethed in the crater below.
  • The ocean seethed and churned during the storm.

Notice it's not just gentle simmering. Seethe implies violent, churning movement — like something is agitated from within.

2. Figurative — Feeling intense, barely-suppressed anger (the most common modern use)

This is how seethe is used most often today, and it's the meaning you'll need to know best.

When a person seethes, they are experiencing anger that is intense, deep, and burning on the inside — but crucially, it is often held back rather than openly exploded. The anger is right there, boiling furiously beneath the surface. They may look calm on the outside, but inside, they are in turmoil.

Think of it as the opposite of a tantrum. A tantrum is explosive and outward. Seething is a fire that burns silently but fiercely within.

  • She smiled and nodded during the meeting, but inside she was seething.
  • He said nothing, but his jaw was tight and his eyes were cold — he was seething.
  • After being humiliated in front of everyone, she seethed for days.

Key qualities of seething anger:

  • It is intense — not mild irritation, but deep, hot anger.
  • It is sustained — it simmers and lingers. You don't seethe for two seconds. You seethe for hours, days, or longer.
  • It is often suppressed or controlled — the person may not be yelling or crying, but the anger is enormous on the inside.
  • It can be visible in subtle ways — in a clenched jaw, cold eyes, clipped speech, or a forced calm.

You can also seethe with a specific emotion:

  • He seethed with rage.
  • She seethed with resentment after years of being overlooked.

3. Figurative — A place or thing teeming with moving activity

A third, less personal use of seethe describes a place or surface that is crowded and churning with movement — like a mass of things writhing or swarming together. This again echoes the image of boiling liquid, where countless bubbles move all at once.

  • The jungle floor seethed with insects.
  • The marketplace seethed with people pushing and shouting.
  • The pit seethed with snakes.

Here, the word gives a sense of overwhelming, agitated, almost disturbing movement — not just "many things," but many things in restless, churning motion.
How Seething Differs from Similar Words

This is where a lot of learners get confused, so let's be precise.

Angry is a broad, general word. You can be mildly angry, deeply angry — it doesn't tell you much beyond the emotion itself.

Furious means openly, intensely angry — usually expressed outwardly and in the moment. It's hot and immediate.

Seething adds two specific layers that the others lack:

  1. The anger is contained or suppressed, not necessarily exploding outward.
  2. It simmers and persists — it doesn't flash and disappear.

So: someone who is furious might be shouting and slamming doors right now. Someone who is seething might be sitting perfectly still, saying nothing, but burning with a deep, churning anger that has been building and won't let go.
The Word "Seething" Used as a Describing Word

You'll very commonly see seething used to describe something in a state of intense agitation:

  • a seething crowd — a massive, agitated, churning crowd
  • seething anger — anger that is intense and barely controlled
  • seething resentment — bitterness that has built up and burns quietly
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

SenseWhat it meansExample

Seethe = to churn violently inside. Literally, of a liquid boiling. Figuratively, of a person burning with intense, suppressed, lingering anger. Or of a place crowded with restless, agitated movement.

The one idea that runs through every use of this word is this: something is at a high intensity, churning from within, and barely contained. Whether it's lava, rage, or a crowd — if it seethes, it is turbulent, restless, and full of barely-held energy.
14367:
When someone is seething, they are experiencing an intense, burning anger — but crucially, that anger is usually held inside, not erupting outward. Think of it as a fury that is churning within a person, barely under control. The person may look calm on the outside, but on the inside, they are boiling.

This is the most common and important meaning of the word. If someone says "she was seething," it tells you two things at once: the anger is very powerful, and it is being suppressed or contained — at least for the moment.

The word carries the image of boiling liquid — water that is not gently warm, but actively churning, bubbling, roiling with heat. That image maps perfectly onto emotion: when someone is seething, their anger is not a cool, still feeling. It is hot, restless, and turbulent inside them.

This is why "seething" feels more vivid than just saying "very angry." It gives you a physical picture: something that is constantly moving, building pressure, ready to overflow.
The Key Quality: Suppressed but Intense

This is the most important nuance to understand. The word "seething" almost always suggests that the anger is not being fully expressed outwardly. The person is holding it in, but with great difficulty. Consider:

He sat silently through the entire meeting, seething.

The silence is part of what makes the word fit. If he were shouting and throwing things, you might call him "furious" or "enraged." But "seething" captures that particular state where the anger is volcanic on the inside yet controlled — or barely controlled — on the outside.

This is why you often see phrases like:

  • "She was seething beneath the surface."
  • "He gave a polite reply, but he was seething."
  • "She smiled, but inwardly she was seething with resentment."

The contrast between the outer composure and the inner fire is exactly what the word is built for.
How It Is Used in Sentences

With a person as subject:

  • After his boss stole credit for his project, he spent the rest of the day seething.
  • She arrived at the party seething, having just received an unfair criticism.

With "with" to name the emotion:

  • He was seething with rage.
  • She was seething with resentment and had been for weeks.

You can say someone is simply "seething" (without naming the emotion, since anger is assumed), or you can be specific using "seething with [emotion]."

As a modifier before a noun (less common but valid):

  • A seething fury built up in her chest.
  • He kept his seething anger hidden from his colleagues.
A Secondary Meaning: Packed and Swarming

There is a second, related meaning. A place can be described as seething when it is very crowded and full of movement — people or things packed together, all in motion, like boiling liquid in a pot.

  • The stadium was seething with excited fans.
  • Below them, the city streets were a seething mass of people.

Notice the phrase "seething with" here too — it means "completely full of" or "teeming with." This meaning is less common in everyday conversation but appears in writing, especially when describing large crowds in an active, almost chaotic state.

Understanding a word fully means knowing when to pick it over its neighbors.

Angry — the general word; covers everything from mild annoyance to intense rage. No particular nuance about whether it's suppressed or expressed.

Furious — very strong, intense anger. Unlike "seething," this word doesn't suggest the anger is hidden; someone furious may be shouting, acting out, or openly upset.

Livid — also very strong anger, often with a sense that it is plainly visible (livid originally referred to a color, like the flush of anger on the face). More about the outward intensity.

Fuming — angry in a way that suggests you are visibly agitated; like steam coming off something. Similar to seething but slightly more cartoonish and less intense.

Seething — the word you choose when the anger is intense and churning internally, suppressed but powerful, like a pressure cooker. It emphasizes the inner experience more than the outer expression.

"Seething" is a moderately formal and literary word. You will encounter it in novels, journalism, and in everyday conversation when someone wants to describe strong emotion with precision. It is not slang. It is not too formal to use in conversation. It sits comfortably in both written and spoken English.

Seething = intensely angry in a way that is churning inside and barely contained. The image is of boiling — hot, turbulent, under pressure. The key quality that separates it from just "very angry" is that the anger is internal, held in, simmering. It can also describe a place that is packed and swarming with movement, but the emotional meaning is far more common and important to know.

A segment is a distinct part of something larger — a clearly defined piece that belongs to a whole, where the whole can be naturally or logically divided into such pieces.

Think of an orange. When you peel it, it splits into those individual curved wedges. Each wedge is a segment. Notice a few things about that example: each piece is clearly defined, they are separate from each other, they are all part of the same whole (the orange), and together they make up the complete thing. That is the heart of what "segment" means.

The word "segment" is not just any word for a "part." It carries a specific feeling: the idea that the whole thing is naturally or logically divisible into these pieces. A segment isn't a random, messy chunk — it implies a clean, recognizable division.

Compare these two sentences:

  • "A segment of the road was damaged." — This suggests a clearly defined section of the road.
  • "A bit of the road was damaged." — This is vaguer and less precise.

"Segment" gives a sense of order and definition to the part being described.
How "Segment" Is Used in Different Areas

The word travels across many fields, but its core meaning stays the same everywhere: a defined part of a whole.

1. Everyday life

You can refer to any clearly defined section of something as a segment.

  • "She watched only the first segment of the documentary." — a defined portion of the film.
  • "A large segment of the crowd left early." — a clear portion of the people.
  • "He focused on just one segment of the problem." — a specific, defined part of an issue.

2. Food

This is probably the most visual example. A grapefruit, orange, or tangerine divides naturally into segments. Each individual wedge-shaped piece is a segment. This is the image to hold in your mind whenever you forget what the word means.

3. Business and Marketing

Companies divide their customers into groups based on things like age, income, location, or interests. Each group is called a market segment.

  • "The luxury segment of the car market grew last year." — referring to the group of buyers who purchase expensive cars.

This usage captures the idea perfectly: the entire market (the whole) is divided into smaller, well-defined groups (segments), and businesses target one or more of these groups.

4. Media and Broadcasting

A TV show, radio program, or podcast is often divided into distinct parts. Each part is a segment.

  • "The news anchor introduced the next segment on climate change."
  • "The cooking segment was everyone's favourite part of the show."

Each segment has its own topic, its own beginning and end — it is a clear, contained piece of the larger program.

5. Mathematics and Geometry

In geometry, a line segment is a portion of a straight line that has a clear starting point and a clear ending point. Unlike a full line, which goes on forever in both directions, a line segment is finite and bounded — it is a defined piece of a line.

A circle segment refers to the region enclosed between a straight line (called a chord) that cuts across a circle and the curved arc of the circle that it cuts off. Imagine slicing a circle the way you'd cut a piece off a hard-boiled egg — the smaller piece you cut off is a segment of the circle.

6. Biology

The bodies of many animals — such as worms, caterpillars, and insects — are made up of repeating ring-like divisions. Each division is called a segment. If you look at a worm, you can clearly see the individual rings that make up its body. Each ring is a segment.

To fully understand the word, keep these qualities in mind whenever you encounter it:

It is a part, not the whole. A segment never refers to the entire thing — always to a piece of it.

It is defined and bounded. A segment has a clear beginning and end, or clear borders. It is not vague or fuzzy.

It belongs to a larger structure. A segment only makes sense in relation to the whole it comes from. You cannot have a segment without something larger that it is a segment of.

The whole can be divided into multiple segments. Usually, when you talk about one segment, there are other segments alongside it. An orange has many segments, not just one. A TV show has multiple segments. A market has multiple segments.

• "a segment of the population" — a defined group of people within society
  • "market segment" — a specific group of customers
  • "a segment of a show/program" — a distinct section of a broadcast
  • "line segment" — a portion of a line with two endpoints
  • "a segment of the journey" — a defined portion of a trip
  • "customer segment" — a group of customers sharing common characteristics
One Sentence to Remember It By

A segment is a clean, well-defined part of a larger whole — like a single wedge of an orange, a section of a TV show, or a specific group within a market.

Hold that orange wedge in your mind, and you will always know what "segment" means.

To segregate means to separate someone or something from the rest of a group and keep them apart — usually based on a specific characteristic, category, or identity.

Think of it this way: imagine a big mixed jar of red and blue marbles. If you pick out all the red ones and put them in their own separate jar, away from the blue ones, you have segregated them. You didn't just remove them — you divided them into distinct, isolated groups based on one defining feature.

That is the heart of the word: deliberate separation that creates a divide.

When used about people — which is its most common and most important use — to segregate means to force a group of people to live, work, study, travel, or exist separately from others, based on something like their race, religion, gender, or caste.

The key word here is force. Segregation isn't just two groups choosing to sit on different sides of a room. It is a system — often backed by law, authority, or social pressure — where one group has the power to push another group away and keep them excluded from shared spaces, opportunities, and rights.

For example: in the United States for much of the 20th century, Black Americans were segregated from white Americans. They were made to attend separate schools, sit in separate sections of buses and restaurants, use separate bathrooms and water fountains. This wasn't a free choice — it was enforced by law. That system was called racial segregation, and dismantling it was one of the central struggles of the Civil Rights Movement.

So when you use "segregate" about people, it almost always carries a heavy, negative weight. It implies injustice, exclusion, and the stripping away of someone's dignity and equal standing in society. It suggests that the separation isn't natural or neutral — it is imposed on the weaker group by the more powerful one.

Segregate is also used in more neutral, everyday contexts when talking about non-human things. Here, it simply means to sort or divide things into separate categories or groups.

For example: a scientist might segregate data into different groups to study them separately. A waste management system might segregate recyclable material from general trash. A bank might segregate different types of funds into separate accounts so they don't mix.

In these cases, the word doesn't carry the dark moral weight it does when applied to people. It's more technical and descriptive — just meaning "to keep these things in separate, distinct categories." Even so, the core idea is the same: you are actively creating a division and maintaining it.
What Makes It Different From Just "Separate"

You might wonder: isn't "segregate" just a fancy word for "separate"? Not quite.

"Separate" is neutral. You can separate eggs from their shells while cooking. You can separate your laundry into darks and lights. There's no power, prejudice, or social meaning implied.

"Segregate," especially when used about people, carries an implication of systemic exclusion. It suggests that the separation is happening at a group level, that it is being imposed rather than chosen, and that it creates inequality. The separated group is not just in a different place — they are in a lesser place, cut off from resources, freedoms, or dignity that others enjoy.

So while all segregation involves separation, not all separation is segregation.
The Connotation: Why the Word Feels Heavy

Because of its deep historical association with racial injustice, the word "segregate" almost always feels serious and uncomfortable when applied to people. Using it signals that you are describing something troubling — an unfair divide, a system that keeps people apart based on who they are rather than anything they've done.

Even in modern usage, if someone says a school "segregates" students by ability level, or a company "segregates" employees by gender in terms of pay or opportunity, it immediately raises a moral alarm. The word asks you to look critically at the separation and question whether it is fair.
Closely Related Forms of the Word

Since you want a complete picture, here are the other forms of this word you'll encounter:

Segregation is the noun form. It refers to the system, act, or condition of being segregated. "Racial segregation was widespread in the American South" — here, segregation names the whole system of forced separation.

Segregated is the adjective form. It describes something that has been or is kept separate. "A segregated school" means a school that only admits students of one race or group.

Desegregate is the opposite action — to end a system of segregation and allow previously separated groups to mix freely and equally. "The Supreme Court ordered schools to desegregate" means the court ordered the removal of the system that kept students apart by race.

Desegregation is the noun form of that — the process of ending segregation.

Here are some sentences that show the word in action across different contexts:

"The apartheid government actively segregated Black and white South Africans in almost every area of public life."

"The hospital chose to segregate patients with infectious diseases in a separate wing to prevent the spread of illness."

"Critics argued that the new housing policy would effectively segregate low-income families into under-resourced neighborhoods."

"The researcher segregated the test results by age group so she could compare outcomes more precisely."

"History shows that whenever a society segregates a group of people based on their identity, inequality follows."

To segregate is to deliberately separate a person, group, or set of things from others and keep them apart — and when applied to people, it almost always means doing so unjustly, based on identity, through the force of law or social power.
